methodological_rigor.justification: Single-center retrospective cohort (n=50) of radiation-induced head/neck malignancies treated 2003-2024 at National Cancer Institute Milan. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis with log-rank testing comparing surgical vs non-surgical treatment. Comparison by margin status (R0 vs R1 vs R2) with appropriate survival stratification. Limitations: retrospective design, incomplete radiotherapy dosimetry data for majority, missing chemotherapy regimen details, small sample with unequal subgroups (n=33 surgery vs n=17 systemic only, n=1 R2 resection), no multivariate adjustment for confounders, no external validation.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Retrospective case series (LoE 4) characterizing rare late complication of radiotherapy. Addresses clinically important population requiring lifelong surveillance. Demonstrates clear survival benefit of surgery (5-year OS 57.5% vs 0%), informing treatment approach for RIM. Clinical relevance limited by single-center setting and retrospective documentation gaps.

reporting_quality.justification: Retrospective cohort study without standard checklist (closest STROBE-aligned for observational work). Methods describe inclusion/exclusion criteria, radiotherapy techniques, outcomes definitions. Results presented with Kaplan-Meier curves stratified by treatment and margin status, demographic/clinical characteristics in tables. Limitations transparently acknowledged: incomplete radiotherapy dosimetry (specific doses unavailable for RIM sites in many cases), missing fractionation details, heterogeneous treatment protocols. Data availability: no statement on data repository access.

novelty_literature.justification: Single-center series of 50 radiation-induced head/neck malignancies demonstrating superior survival with surgery (established finding in prior literature). Confirms known dose-response patterns (sarcomas in high-dose regions 45% vs SCC in intermediate-dose 27%) and latency correlations with age at treatment. Limited novelty beyond descriptive epidemiologic characterization of rare complication.

writing_presentation.justification: Well-organized retrospective series with clear clinical motivation establishing importance of long-term surveillance after RT. Methods and results transparently presented. Discussion comprehensively addresses diagnostic challenges in irradiated tissue (fibrosis, edema masking tumors), treatment complexities, and provides detailed literature context. Representative clinical cases enhance clarity. Publication-ready organization despite methodological limitations.

key_strengths: Demonstrates clear survival advantage of surgical treatment (5-year OS 57.5%) versus systemic therapy alone (0%), supporting surgery as cornerstone of RIM management even when complete resection not achievable (non-radical surgery 36% 5-yr OS vs 0% systemic only)

Transparently acknowledges methodological limitations including incomplete radiotherapy dosimetry for majority (specific doses at RIM sites unavailable), missing fractionation details, and heterogeneous treatment protocols across 21-year period

Provides clinical insights on diagnostic challenges in irradiated tissue (fibrosis, edema, submucosal presentation) contributing to delayed diagnosis at advanced stages, with 22% requiring multiple biopsies for confirmation

Describes histologic distribution patterns: smokers with RIM show heterogeneous distribution (SCC 44%, sarcoma 44%) versus non-smokers (SCC 65%, sarcoma 23%), supporting radiation-driven carcinogenesis distinct from tobacco patterns
key_concerns: Single-center monocentric design from specialized tertiary institute with potential referral bias; limited generalizability; small sample (n=50) with unequal treatment groups (n=33 surgery, n=17 systemic only, n=1 R2 resection) restricts statistical power

Incomplete radiotherapy data significantly limits analysis: specific doses at RIM onset sites unavailable for many patients, preventing dose-response validation; missing fractionation details despite emerging interest in hypofractionation effects

Retrospective design introduces heterogeneity in surgical and systemic treatment over 21-year period with evolving standards; no multivariate adjustment for treatment selection bias or other confounders

Small margin-status subgroups limit definitive comparisons (R2 group n=1); authors acknowledge survival trends in margin analysis not statistically significant (p=0.18) due to limited sample; no external validation cohort
chief_reviewer.rationale: Descriptive single-center retrospective series documenting rare radiation-induced head/neck malignancies with clear surgical benefit, but incomplete radiotherapy dosimetry, small unequal treatment groups, and lack of external validation limit tier to 4. Appropriate for specialty journals documenting rare disease outcomes with appropriate caveats.
